column4: This verse says that spending is for the giver, must be done seeking God's face, and will be repaid in full by God. It makes the section's claim that no human favor is being repaid especially concrete: the giver seeks God, not a debtor's return.

This verse calls wealth and children a trial; 64:16 follows by telling people to spend from what God provided and resist stinginess. Its own contribution is to frame the section's property and giving choice as a test.

The verse warns believers not to let wealth and children distract them from God's remembrance. It identifies a particular way possession can obstruct the giving and devotion that distinguish the section's two paths.
This verse tells people to spend from what God provided before death comes. It connects the section's held wealth and its failure at the end with an urgent opportunity to give while one still has it.
This closes the warning in 63:9–10 by saying God will not delay a soul when its appointed time comes. Its own contribution is the finality that makes spending before death consequential.

The verse says not to covet what God has given some over others and that each has a share of what they earn (نَصِيبٌ مِمَّا اكْتَسَبُوا). It gives an earned portion as a counterpart to the section's share won by lot.
After people ask for good in both lives, this verse says each has a share of what they earned. It connects the section's dictionary sense of share to outcomes grounded in conduct rather than a draw.
This verse sets distinct inheritance portions for children and parents. It gives a concrete example of measured property shares assigned by rule, unlike the section's chance-drawn division.

The verse assigns fixed inheritance portions to spouses and certain siblings. It continues the measured divisions in 4:11 and shows the section's idea of apportioned shares applied to property by rule.
This verse assigns a fifth of war gains to named recipients, including the needy and orphans. It is another material-share scene where the portion is prescribed, not won by arrows.

This verse directs distribution of communal gains to named recipients so wealth will not circulate only among the rich. It gives a social rule for sharing property, contrasting with the section's lot-drawn winner.
The verse describes the God-conscious as spending in both prosperity and adversity. It makes the section's giving a chosen stance across circumstances, not an ease that depends on chance.

The verse criticizes people who claim purity for themselves and says God purifies whom He wills. It places a boundary around the section's giver who gives to purify himself: purification is not a self-awarded possession.

This verse distinguishes the rank of those who spent and fought before victory from those who acted later, while promising good to both. It links rank to costly action rather than to the section's highest arrow winning a share.
The verse pictures spending in God's way as seed yielding multiplied grain. It gives a concrete return from giving, in contrast to seeking material gain through the section's chance-based game.
